title: Got an Unsolicited Offer?
metaTitle: Got a Mailbox Offer for Your WV Mineral Rights?
metaDescription: Received an unsolicited letter offering to buy your West Virginia mineral rights? We benchmark it against your actual title and unit activity before you sign.
heroLead: A letter offering to buy your West Virginia mineral rights out of nowhere usually means someone has already looked at the county records and decided the number is worth chasing.
intro: Mailbox offers on West Virginia mineral rights tend to arrive in waves, usually right after a new permit is filed, a unit is designated, or an operator's leasing activity picks up in a county. Whoever sent the letter has typically pulled your name and tract directly from the county clerk's recorded index, which means they already know something about your interest's location and, often, its production or leasing status, before you've had a chance to look into it yourself.

We don't think every unsolicited offer is unfair, but we do think owners deserve to know what their interest is actually worth before signing anything a stranger mailed them. We'll review the letter and your documentation and tell you honestly where it stands.

sections.heading: Why the letter showed up when it did
paragraphs: If you just received an offer, it's worth checking whether a new well permit was recently filed on or near your tract, whether a unit designation order was recorded that includes your acreage, or whether nearby leasing activity picked up. Buyers who send these letters are often working from exactly that kind of trigger, meaning the timing itself can tell you something about why your interest suddenly looks attractive, information the letter itself usually doesn't share.
We check the same public records to see what prompted the interest, then explain it to you directly rather than leaving you to guess.

sections.heading: Reading the actual terms rather than the headline number
paragraphs: Some unsolicited offers quote a number that sounds reasonable on its face but attach it to unfavorable terms buried in the fine print, a long due diligence period with no real obligation on the buyer's side, a right to renegotiate the price after their own title review, or a deed that conveys more than what the letter described, sometimes including future formations or interests the seller didn't intend to give up. We read the actual purchase agreement in full, beyond the cover letter, and flag anything that doesn't match what was advertised.
This isn't unique to any one company, it's common enough in mineral buying generally that reading the full document before signing is worth the time regardless of who sent it.

sections.heading: Getting a real benchmark before you respond
paragraphs: We'll pull the same recorded lease and title information the letter-writer likely used and give you our own assessment of what your interest is worth, based on your unit's actual activity, your lease terms, and recent comparable transfers where available. You're under no obligation to sell to us just because you asked for a comparison, and having a second, documented number in hand puts you in a stronger position whether you ultimately sell to the original buyer, to us, or decide not to sell at all right now.

sections.heading: What to do before signing anything
paragraphs: Don't sign or return a mailed offer on deadline pressure alone. Legitimate buyers will give you time to have the offer reviewed. Pull your own copy of the deed and any lease from the county clerk's office if you don't already have one, and get at least one independent comparison before committing your interest to any single buyer's terms, especially if the letter arrived with a short response window attached.

faqs.question: Is it normal to get an unsolicited offer for mineral rights I've owned for years?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially after a new permit, unit designation, or leasing activity near your tract. It's usually a sign someone has flagged renewed interest in your area, not that your title has a problem.

faqs.question: Should I just sign the offer that showed up in my mailbox?
faqs.answer: Not without reading the full purchase agreement and getting at least one comparison. The headline price can look reasonable while other terms in the document work against you.

faqs.question: How do I know if the offer price is fair?
faqs.answer: We can review your lease and title records and give you our own documented number based on your unit's actual activity, so you have something concrete to compare the offer against.

faqs.question: Do I have to sell to you just because I asked for a comparison?
faqs.answer: No. There's no obligation. Plenty of owners use our review simply to have an independent number before deciding whether to accept, negotiate, or decline the original offer.

faqs.question: What should I watch for in the fine print of a mailed offer?
faqs.answer: Long due diligence periods with a one-sided right to renegotiate price, deed language that conveys more than what the letter described, and vague depth or formation language are the most common issues worth reading closely before signing.

faqs.question: How quickly do I need to respond to an unsolicited offer?
faqs.answer: There's rarely a real reason to rush. A legitimate buyer will hold the offer open long enough for you to have it reviewed, and we can usually turn around a comparison within a few days once we have your documentation.
